publish.title: What Is a Seed Phrase? How to Store It Safely (Beginner Guide)
publish.description:
What is a seed phrase, and how do you store it safely? In this beginner guide: what those 12 or 24 words really are, why they are your money and not just a password, the scams built to steal them (fake "validate your wallet" pages, screenshot-scanning apps, the shared-seed trap, seed checker sites), and a simple way to write, store and protect your backup.

{chapters}

This video is for educational purposes only and is not financial advice.

#seedphrase #crypto #cryptoforbeginners

scenes.name: hook
narration: Twelve simple words. River, anchor, pilot, velvet.
To most people, they look like a random shopping list.
But if a stranger reads those words, he can take every coin in your wallet, from anywhere in the world, in about a minute.
No password, no code, no permission needed.
In this video, you'll learn what a seed phrase really is, the tricks scammers use to get it, and exactly how to store it safely.

elements.sub: what it is and how to store it safely

scenes.name: what-is
narration: So what is a seed phrase?
When you create a crypto wallet, the app gives you twelve or twenty-four words, in a fixed order.
Those words come from a standard list of two thousand and forty-eight simple English words.
Together, they are a human-readable backup of your private key, the secret that controls your coins.
The last word even works as a checksum, so a wallet can usually spot a word that's wrong.
One important note: if your crypto sits on an exchange account, you don't have a seed phrase. The exchange holds the keys.
Seed phrases come with self-custody wallets, apps or devices where you hold the key yourself.

widgets.text: Write down these words in order

scenes.name: your-money
narration: Here is the part that surprises beginners.
Your wallet app is just a window. The coins live on the blockchain.
If you lose your phone, you install a wallet on a new one, type the twelve words, and everything is back.
That's great news for you.
But it works exactly the same way for anyone else who types those words.
There is no reset button, no support line and no bank that can reverse it.
So your seed phrase isn't a password to your money. It is your money.

elements.text: Your app is just a window

scenes.name: guessing
narration: You might wonder: can't a hacker just guess the twelve words?
No. With two thousand and forty-eight options for every single word, the number of possible combinations is astronomical.
Every computer on Earth working together couldn't try them all.
So attackers don't guess your seed phrase. They trick you into handing it over, or they find where you saved it.
Every scam in this video works that way. It attacks you, not the math.
And the first one fools even careful people.

elements.text: they attack you, not the math

scenes.name: rule1-nobody-asks
narration: Rule number one: nobody legitimate will ever ask for your seed phrase.
Not your wallet's support team. Not your exchange. Not a website, an app update or an airdrop.
A real wallet asks for those words in exactly one situation: when you choose to restore your wallet yourself, inside the official app.
If anyone else asks, in a chat, an email, a form or a phone call, the conversation is over.
That one rule blocks most seed phrase scams on its own.
Now let's look at how scammers try to get around it.

elements.text: Anyone asks = scam. End the conversation.

scenes.name: scam1-validate
narration: Scam number one: the validate your wallet page.
You get an email, a pop-up or a message that looks like it's from your wallet.
It says your wallet must be synced, validated or upgraded, or it will be locked.
Scammers have even mailed printed letters to hardware wallet owners, with a QR code that leads to a fake page.
The page looks official, and it asks you to type your twelve or twenty-four words.
The moment you press submit, the scammer has a full copy of your wallet.
How to spot it: real wallets never need to be validated, and they never set deadlines. Close the page.

widgets.text: Your wallet must be validated within 24 hours or it will be locked.

scenes.name: scam2-screenshots
narration: Scam number two doesn't even need you to type anything.
Many beginners take a screenshot or a photo of their seed phrase, just to be safe.
In twenty twenty-five, security researchers found apps in both major app stores that secretly scanned people's photo galleries.
They used text recognition to find recovery phrases in screenshots, and sent them to attackers.
Photos also sync to the cloud, so one hacked cloud account can expose them too.
So never photograph your seed phrase, and never screenshot it.
And the next scam is the sneakiest, because it looks like free money.

elements.text: found in both major app stores

scenes.name: scam3-shared-seed
narration: Scam number three flips the trick around. Here, the scammer gives you a seed phrase.
You see a comment where someone accidentally posts their twelve words, next to a wallet holding thousands of dollars in tokens.
You import the words, and the balance is real.
But to move the tokens, you first need a little crypto to pay the network fee.
So you send twenty dollars for the fee, and an automatic program drains it the second it arrives.
The same idea hides in a hardware wallet that arrives with words already filled in.
Rule: never use a seed phrase that someone else gave you, or that you didn't create yourself.

lines.text: Help! How do I move this to my exchange?
orbit frost maple candle river lunar ...

scenes.name: scam4-checker
narration: Scam number four: seed phrase checker and generator websites.
You want to check whether your backup is valid, so you search, and you find a free online tool.
Or a site offers to generate a stronger seed phrase for you.
Either way, the words pass through someone else's server, and that server can keep them.
Your wallet is the only place where your seed phrase should ever be created or typed.
No website, no matter how helpful it looks.

widgets.text: Paste your 12 words to check them

scenes.name: story-alex
narration: Now imagine Alex. He's careful. He never shares his words with anyone.
When he set up his wallet, he typed the seed phrase into his notes app, so he wouldn't lose it.
The notes synced to his cloud account, which used the same password as an old shopping site.
That shopping site got breached, and attackers tried the leaked password everywhere.
They logged into his cloud, searched his notes for wallet words, and found them.
Alex didn't click a single scam link. His backup was the hole.
So the next part is the most important one: how to store your seed phrase so this can't happen to you.

widgets.text: river anchor pilot velvet harbor ember lunar maple orbit candle frost willow

scenes.name: step1-write
narration: Step one: write it down on paper, by hand.
Do it when you create the wallet, in a private place, with no cameras around and no one watching.
Number every word, one to twelve or one to twenty-four, because the order matters.
Write clearly, and double-check the spelling against the screen.
Many wallets then ask you to confirm a few words. Don't skip that test.
And never type the words into anything except the wallet itself: no notes, no email, no document.
Paper can't be hacked from the other side of the world.

scenes.name: step2-where
narration: Step two: choose where it lives.
Keep at least two copies, in two different safe places. For example, a locked drawer at home, and a second place you trust, like a bank safe deposit box.
Paper can burn, get wet or fade. So for larger amounts, many people stamp or engrave the words on a metal backup plate.
Don't label it crypto seed phrase in big letters.
And make sure one person you trust knows how to find it if something happens to you.
The goal is simple: hard to steal, hard to destroy, possible to find.

scenes.name: myth-split
narration: Now, a popular idea that sounds smart: splitting the phrase in half.
Six words here, six words there. If a thief finds one half, he's stuck, right?
The problem: lose either half, and your wallet is gone for good.
Homemade schemes like this make mistakes more likely, not less.
If you want an extra layer, there is a better, built-in tool.
It's called the passphrase, and some people call it the twenty-fifth word.

scenes.name: tip-passphrase
narration: Many wallets support an optional passphrase.
It's an extra secret that you add on top of your seed phrase.
With it, the same twelve words open a completely different wallet.
So if someone finds your paper, without the passphrase they can't reach your main funds.
But there is a catch. If you forget the passphrase, nobody can recover it. Not even the wallet maker.
So it's for people who already have a solid backup habit. If you're just starting, master the basics first.

scenes.name: tip-exposed
narration: Last tip: what if you think someone saw your words?
Maybe you typed them on a suspicious site, or you find an old photo of them in your cloud.
Don't wait to see what happens.
Create a brand-new wallet with a brand-new seed phrase, and write it on paper.
Then move everything from the old wallet to the new one, right away.
Treat the old phrase as burned. Never use that wallet again.

scenes.name: recap
narration: Let's recap.
One: your seed phrase is your money, not just a password.
Two: nobody legitimate will ever ask for it.
Three: no screenshots, no photos, no notes app, no cloud.
Four: never use words that someone else gave you.
Five: paper or metal, numbered, at least two copies in two places.
Six: if it leaks, move your funds to a new wallet right away.

items.text: It's your money, not a password
Nobody legit will ever ask for it
No screenshots, photos, notes or cloud
Never use words someone gave you
Leaked? Move funds to a new wallet

scenes.name: outro
narration: If this helped, subscribe.
Next, I'll show you how to tell if a crypto website or app is legit or a scam.
And tell me in the comments: has anyone ever asked you for your seed phrase?
